soil-found-115.q: Where does the critical zone end at depth?
soil-found-115.a: At some depth in bedrock, where life and water cease to change the chemistry significantly.

soil-found-047.q: How long does mineral-associated organic matter typically persist, compared with particulate organic matter?
soil-found-047.a: Typically for centuries, whereas particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

soil-form-097.q: Which part of the regolith is conventionally called soil?
soil-form-097.a: Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter.

soil-form-146.q: What silica content and enrichments mark mafic rocks?
soil-form-146.a: They have 45 to 55 wt% silica and are enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium.

soil-form-105.q: What features typically mark a meandering river?
soil-form-105.a: Point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

soil-form-023.q: Why does the subsoil get most of its colour from iron oxides?
soil-form-023.a: Because it holds little organic matter.

soil-form-019.q: What is the defining feature of Mollisols?
soil-form-019.a: A fertile mollic epipedon, built by long additions of root-derived organic matter.

soil-form-070.q: How much phosphorus did laterite remove from solution in laboratory tests and at pilot scale?
soil-form-070.a: 99% in laboratory tests and 96% in a pilot-scale facility.

soil-form-127.q: Why is phosphorus often the most deficient nutrient in tropical soils?
soil-form-127.a: Intense leaching and weathering deplete the mineral pool, and unlike nitrogen it cannot be replenished from the air.

soil-phys-189.q: How much surface per gram do clay minerals typically have?
soil-phys-189.a: Typically 10 to 1,000 square metres per gram, as they form thin plates.

soil-phys-125.q: Over what range does hydraulic conductivity vary from clays to gravels?
soil-phys-125.a: From about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels.

soil-phys-064.q: Why are clay soils called heavy, despite their high porosity?
soil-phys-064.a: The word reflects their moisture weight and the extra force needed to pull tillage tools through them.

soil-phys-114.q: How is the overconsolidation ratio (OCR) defined?
soil-phys-114.a: It divides the preconsolidation stress, the highest stress a soil has carried, by the current stress.

soil-water-182.q: What theory describes how most soil water enters plants?
soil-water-182.a: The cohesion-tension theory: water is pulled passively up the column of xylem sap from roots to leaves as it transpires.

soil-phys-210.q: What is the general basin form of the water balance?
soil-phys-210.a: P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus change in storage.

soil-water-174.q: Why does a high salt content restrict water uptake by roots?
soil-water-174.a: Solutes lower the osmotic potential of the soil solution, which severely restricts uptake by roots.

soil-phys-221.q: What is the pressure head at the water table?
soil-phys-221.a: There it equals atmospheric pressure; below it pressure head exceeds atmospheric pressure, and above it is negative.

soil-phys-201.q: Why are karst aquifers more sensitive to contamination than porous aquifers?
soil-phys-201.a: Their fast flow, through limestone fissures widened by carbonic acid, makes them far more sensitive.

soil-phys-194.q: Why do less soluble contaminants travel only short distances?
soil-phys-194.a: Adsorption holds them back, so they can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water.

soil-phys-180.q: What does Fick's first law state?
soil-phys-180.a: J = −D dφ/dx: diffusive flux equals the diffusion coefficient times the concentration gradient, with a minus sign.

soil-phys-145.q: How deep do annual temperature cycles penetrate in wet and dry clay?
soil-phys-145.a: About 18.0 m in wet clay but only 6.5 m in dry clay.

soil-chem-107.q: What size are the particles of the colloidal fraction of soil?
soil-chem-107.a: Tiny clay and humus particles under 1 μm across, whose charges vary with soil pH.

soil-chem-097.q: What does allophane alter to when silica is added, and when it is removed?
soil-chem-097.a: To halloysite where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed.

soil-chem-085.q: Why is the cation exchange capacity of kaolinite low?
soil-chem-085.a: Kaolinite has undergone almost no isomorphous substitution.

soil-chem-071.q: How many milliequivalents are 1 mmol of Na+ and 1 mmol of Ca2+?
soil-chem-071.a: 1 milliequivalent for Na+ but 2 for Ca2+, since equivalents are moles multiplied by valence.

soil-chem-130.q: When and where was biofiltration first introduced?
soil-chem-130.a: In England in 1893, as a trickling filter for wastewater.

soil-chem-180.q: Between which two lines is water stable on a Pourbaix diagram?
soil-chem-180.a: Between EH = −0.05916 pH and EH = 1.229 V − 0.05916 pH; outside them it is reduced to hydrogen or oxidized to oxygen.

soil-chem-142.q: How does alkalinity differ from basicity?
soil-chem-142.a: Basicity is an absolute position on the pH scale, while alkalinity is measured by titrating with an acid to an endpoint.

soil-chem-021.q: How does gypsum reclaim an alkali soil?
soil-chem-021.a: It supplies Ca2+ to replace sodium on the exchange complex and turns sodium carbonate into neutral sodium sulphate.

soil-bio-212.a: They are primarily detritivores, eating dead plants at any stage of decay.

soil-bio-071.q: What did a 2007 study find to be the main global determinant of bacterial diversity?

soil-bio-225.q: Which compound gives soil its earthy odour?
soil-bio-225.a: Geosmin, a volatile compound released by soil bacteria that mostly also produce spores.

soil-bio-054.q: How fast do bacteria turn over in the rhizosphere?
soil-bio-054.a: In just 12–19 hours, shorter on younger roots, because root exudates make the rhizosphere a special case.

soil-bio-178.q: What do rhizobia and legumes exchange in their mutualism?
soil-bio-178.a: The bacteria supply ammonia or amino acids and receive organic acids, mainly malate and succinate, as their carbon and energy source.

soil-bio-240.a: Hyphae aggregated into durable, water-repellent transport structures that work like xylem.

soil-bio-248.a: Secreted by mycorrhizal hyphae, it builds stable aggregates that resist erosion and accounts for about 5% of global organic carbon and nitrogen storage.

soil-bio-196.q: Why do autumn leaves decompose more slowly than most compost ingredients?
soil-bio-196.a: They are low in nitrogen and made largely of cellulose and lignin, which resist decay.

soil-bio-258.q: What does the Michaelis constant Km represent?
soil-bio-258.a: The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of the limiting rate V.

soil-class-021.q: What system replaced the FAO soil classification, and when?
soil-class-021.a: The World Reference Base replaced it in 1998.

soil-class-155.q: Where does the ustic moisture regime sit relative to the aridic and udic?
soil-class-155.a: It is wetter than the aridic and drier than the udic.

soil-class-116.q: Which soil order covers the largest share of U.S. land?
soil-class-116.a: Mollisols, at an estimated 21.5%, followed by Alfisols at 14%.

soil-class-139.q: Which soils are excluded from the Regosols?
soil-class-139.a: Weakly developed soils that qualify as Leptosols, Arenosols or Fluvisols; Regosols are a leftover group for soils that fit no other.

soil-class-065.q: Why must fill be as free of organic matter as possible?
soil-class-065.a: Decomposing organic matter leaves voids that make the fill settle and can damage structures built on it.

soil-fert-165.q: At what concentration in soil water is boron toxic to most plants?

soil-fert-195.q: Why does sulfur deficiency show first in the youngest tissues?
soil-fert-195.a: Sulfur cannot be moved out of older leaves, so yellowing and stunting appear first in the youngest tissues.

soil-fert-119.q: What do denitrifying bacteria use in place of oxygen?
soil-fert-119.a: Nitrate and nitrite, as the final electron acceptor.

soil-fert-138.q: What share of soil potassium is in the soil solution, the form plants absorb most readily?
soil-fert-138.a: Only 0.1–0.2% of the total; fixed potassium makes up 96–99%.

soil-fert-082.q: Why does excess salt around roots make a plant respond as in drought?
soil-fert-082.a: When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots.

soil-fert-067.q: Why can straw or sawdust mulch briefly slow plant growth?
soil-fert-067.a: Their wide carbon-to-nitrogen ratio lets decomposing microbes draw nitrogen from the soil.

soil-fert-013.q: What do the numbers of a fertilizer grade such as 10-10-10 give?
soil-fert-013.a: The percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O.

soil-water-079.q: What two fates await rain that reaches land?
soil-water-079.a: It either flows over the ground as surface runoff or soaks in by infiltration, becoming soil moisture or groundwater.

soil-water-083.q: Why are planners advised to avoid karst for new development?
soil-water-083.a: Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses.

soil-water-042.q: Why must drop size and terminal velocity be simulated accurately on bare soil?

soil-water-006.q: How do earth and debris differ in landslide classification?
soil-water-006.a: Earth has less than 20% by weight of particles over 2 mm; debris has more.

soil-water-098.q: Why are anionic flocculants best practice in open systems?
soil-water-098.a: Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish.

soil-water-253.q: What does a well-developed desert pavement indicate?
soil-water-253.a: Aridity and an older surface, since older surfaces carry better-developed pavements.

soil-water-280.q: What share of damaging landslides in the year to September 2003 were triggered by heavy rainfall?

soil-water-267.q: How does tropical peatland forest compare with forest on mineral soil as a carbon store?
soil-water-267.a: It holds far more carbon as soil organic matter, among the largest near-surface stores of land organic carbon.

soil-water-297.q: How do dead plankton help fill in a pond?
soil-water-297.a: They decay into humus that mixes with inwashed silt and clay to form soil, making the pond shallower.

soil-agri-030.q: What is the difference between monoculture and monocropping?
soil-agri-030.a: Monoculture describes crop diversity in space, whereas monocropping describes diversity over time.

soil-agri-011.q: In what units is soil salinity most often expressed?
soil-agri-011.a: As ECe in decisiemens per metre, formerly millimhos per centimetre.

soil-agri-110.q: Why did the heavy carruca plough make farming communal?
soil-agri-110.a: Pulling it took four to eight oxen, more than one peasant household had.

soil-agri-067.a: The ability of cover crops, such as nitrogen-fixing legumes, to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer.

soil-agri-159.q: How wide do filter strips need to be?
soil-agri-159.a: At least 15 feet (4.6 m), and they can often serve as a cheap substitute for terraces.

soil-agri-167.q: What do the two Not Suitable land classes, N1 and N2, mean?
soil-agri-167.a: N1 has limitations that might be overcome in time but not at acceptable cost now; N2 has limitations ruling out any sustained use.

soil-form-020.q: Why do micromorphologists use thin sections rather than a hand lens?
soil-form-020.a: A petrographic polarizing microscope shows far more in thin sections, including the relation of components to one another, often invisible in a hand specimen.

soil-meth-007.q: Which exponent of distance did Shepard settle on for inverse distance weighting?
soil-meth-007.a: Near -2, close to the gravity model.

soil-env-283.q: How can lowering a wetland's water table affect its methane balance?
soil-env-283.a: It increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs and can turn the wetland into a methane sink.

soil-env-085.q: How does contour trenching prevent erosion?
soil-env-085.a: Trenches 150 m long and 1 m deep are dug along the contour and edged with stone walls, so water cannot flow.

soil-env-090.q: How much agricultural land had unsustainable farming degraded by 2025?
soil-env-090.a: 996 Mha, over 60% of all human-induced land degradation.

soil-env-217.q: In what order are materials replaced when an open-cut mine is reclaimed?
soil-env-217.a: Rock backfills the pit, stored pre-mining soil goes on top, then topsoil, and finally vegetation is restored.

soil-env-038.a: Adding a chelator to make heavy metals, often too immobile for plants to absorb, more soluble.

soil-env-034.q: Why can ligninolytic fungi degrade many organic pollutants?
soil-env-034.a: Lignin and cellulose are long-chain carbon compounds much like many organic pollutants.

soil-env-252.q: Which nanoparticle has been used in most field applications of nanoremediation?

soil-env-229.q: Why does electrical resistance heating (ERH) work in any soil type?
soil-env-229.a: Current travels mainly through the thin water film on grains, which is also why it cannot dry the ground out.

soil-env-296.q: How does Finland raise soil selenium?
soil-env-296.a: It adds selenium salts to chemical fertilizers.

soil-hist-127.q: What is the half-life of beryllium-10, and what does it date?
soil-hist-127.a: 1,387,000 years; it dates exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores.

soil-hist-096.q: Who first proposed the law of superposition, and when?

soil-hist-042.q: What did Darwin's chalk experiment near Down House show?
soil-hist-042.a: Chalk spread in December 1842 ended up buried 18 centimetres deep, a rate of 6 millimetres per year.

soil-hist-016.q: Which bacterium was shown in 1901 to fix atmospheric nitrogen?
soil-hist-016.a: Azotobacter chroococcum, in work that fully described the fixation process found by Hellriegel and Wilfarth.

soil-hist-107.q: Which soil did the Wisconsin legislature name the official state soil in 1983?

soil-hist-068.q: How do planetary scientists functionally separate rock from soil?
soil-hist-068.a: Rocks are fragments of about 10 cm or more, larger than cobbles; soil is all other, typically loose material.
